1:
Whether the grief is one man’s or a people’s is settled early and differently. John Calvin denies that any private individual is speaking: the Holy Spirit seems to have dictated a common form of prayer for the Church in her afflictions, and what we hear are the lamentations of the chosen people. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion by inference — the affliction remains obscure, but since the consolation sought is in the earlier revelations of power and mercy in the national history, it cannot be purely personal. Adam Clarke has the author speaking in the persons of the captive Israelites, while allowing that the psalm may be adapted to any individual in spiritual distress; he notes that Asaph and Jeduthun were singers in David’s time whose names were long afterwards borne by the bands they led, but thinks there was also a person of that name in the captivity. Matthew Henry reads it as one man throughout, the portraiture of a good man under prevailing melancholy, in which drooping saints may see their own faces as in a glass. Augustine of Hippo takes the two names of the title etymologically and gets a congregation that leaps over, leaping in order to reach the end, which is Christ.

C.H. Spurgeon notes that the psalm begins with prayer and so cannot end ill; the cry is not studied or stilted but the natural expression of pain, and though vocal utterance is not necessary to the life of prayer it is often forced upon us by the energy of desire, as it is a comfort to hear the alarm-bell ring when the house is invaded. Charles Ellicott would follow the Hebrew literally — my voice to God, and let me cry; my voice to God, and he hears me — and complains that the received version has followed the Greek and Latin in neglecting the striking changes of mood that run through the psalm, soliloquy and narrative alternating as the poet is impelled now to vent his feelings and now to analyse them. Augustine of Hippo asks what the crying is for: many cry to the Lord for riches, for the safety of friends, for temporal felicity, for secular dignity, even for mere soundness of body, which is the poor man’s inheritance, but scarce one cries for the sake of the Lord himself.

The second verse is corrupt or mistranslated, and both close readers say so. Adam Clarke calls the received rendering most unaccountable: the words mean that his hand was stretched out, that is, in prayer, so that he continued the whole night with voice and hands lifted up and did not cease even amid great discouragements. Charles Ellicott goes further and calls the text evidently faulty and as it stands unintelligible; the Greek and Latin point to a different reading, Symmachus gives the stretched-out hand, and a comparison with the Lamentations suggests that eye was written where we now have hand, while the sore of our version comes from the Rabbins, who thought of a hand beating the breast. The probable text, he concludes, may be beyond recovery, though the feeling of the verse is palpable, and he gives it in a couplet on vows in the night, fierce and unavailing. John Gill leaves the text alone and asks instead why remembering God should trouble a man: because he recalls his own ingratitude for so much kindness, or because he contrasts former grace with present want of it, or rather because he remembers the greatness, power and holiness of God and himself as sinful dust, considering him not as father and friend but as an angry Judge. John Wesley says the same shorter, that the thoughts of God were now matter of trouble because he was angry.
4:
Whether the eyes are held open or held shut divides the entry at once. Charles Ellicott says the received version mistakes the noun for a participle and turns a passive into an active: the words are that God has closed the guards of his eyes, meaning the eyelids, the verb being used elsewhere of God veiling his throne in cloud and so shutting it from the access of men. Adam Clarke keeps the waking and renders it that God keeps the watches of his eyes, the grief being too great for sleep. John Gill reaches the same sense by another road, taking the word for the keepers of the eyes, that is the eyebrows, held so that he could not shut them. C.H. Spurgeon makes the eyes sentinels forbidden to rest and asks what anodyne can give rest if God himself holds them waking. On the speechlessness that follows Adam Clarke observes that at first the psalmist felt his misery and cried aloud, but that as he sees more of his wretchedness his words are swallowed by distress, and quotes the maxim that small troubles are loquacious while great ones are dumb. Charles Ellicott finds a different cause: the verb is used elsewhere of the awestruck state produced by a mysterious dream, and the poet has been struck dumb and is too overawed to speak.

Adam Clarke doubts the received rendering of the song in the night as well, since the word signifies a stringed instrument struck with a plectrum; he supposes the psalmist to be describing the composition of the short ode that follows, sung to the harp as a kind of dirge — if indeed, he adds, he had a harp in that distressful captivity. Charles Ellicott renders the lines as a series of resolutions: let me recall my harpings in the night, let me complain in my own heart, and my spirit questions and questions. C.H. Spurgeon makes the recollection a duty rather than an indulgence, memory ransacking the past for a light to borrow, though he notes that even this created depression rather than delight. Adam Clarke presses the verb for searching, which describes the kind of investigation a man makes who must strip himself to do it, leaving no fold unlifted, and notes in passing that the Latin word used to translate it is no pure Latin at all and occurs in no author but one.

The questions that follow are read as unbelief by some and as faith by others, and John Gill reports all three positions from the versions: the Syriac turns them into affirmations and so speaks unbelief, the Arabic makes them a subject of inquiry and so at most doubt, while the Targum opens each with is it possible that the Lord, which implies that it is not, and so speaks faith. He then answers each question twice over, once as Unbelief says and once as Faith says. Adam Clarke treats them as pleading and reasoning with his Maker, and asks whether there will be no end to the captivity. On the shutting up of the tender mercies he takes the figure from a spring whose mouth is closed, so that the water breaks out and takes another course, and answers the question in the affirmative: God did take his mercy from the Jews and give it to the Gentiles. John Wesley reads the casting off as concerning his peculiar people rather than the psalmist alone.
10:
The tenth verse is the obscurest in the psalm and produces five answers. Adam Clarke reports two Latin renderings: one derives the verb from a root meaning to pray and gives, to pray, this is my business; to change belongs to the right hand of the Most High; the other gives, to grieve is my portion, to change my condition belongs to the right hand of the Most High, taking the word we render years from a root meaning to change. He prefers the second, and sums the verse as, I am in deep distress, and the Most High alone can change my condition; he adds his old Psalter’s rendering, which follows the Latin and begins, now I began this changing of the right hand of the highest. Charles Ellicott starts from the noun, which by derivation may mean a wounding or a piercing, and which the old Greek translators gave as my wound and my sickness; on that reading it is mental sickness, and the poet says that to indulge despairing cries is mere madness, for which he cites the king in the play who says that way madness lies. But he prefers the sense the cognate verb commonly bears and renders it profanation: to despair of continued help from one who had been so gracious in the past is a kind of blasphemy. John Gill allows the verse to be either self-correction or self-comfort — a confession that questioning God’s love is a besetting sin, or an assurance that the trouble is a sickness but not to death. C.H. Spurgeon notes how much our translators supply, the original consisting only of the words about the years of the right hand of the Most High, and takes the sense to be that the long affliction was allotted by the Sovereign Lord.

On the resolution to remember Charles Ellicott notes that the written text has I will celebrate rather than I will remember, though the intention is the same, and that works and wonders should be singular, referring to the one mighty deliverance from Egypt which occupies the poet’s thoughts. John Gill reports the same double reading and takes the alternative to mean declaring the works to others. Matthew Henry draws the lesson from the repetition, that it is good to persevere in the proper means for strengthening faith even when they do not prove effectual at first, since the psalmist had tried this remedy already and failed, and tried again and succeeded. C.H. Spurgeon bids the soul fly back from present turmoils to the grandeurs of history.

Where God’s way is divides the last verses. Adam Clarke keeps the sanctuary and makes it practical: he must go there now to get comfort as he went before to get instruction, and asks how many doubts have been solved and fears dissipated while waiting on God in the means of grace; he allows the alternative that the way is in holiness. Charles Ellicott takes it neither way, rendering it with the holy, that is with Israel, the saint of God. John Gill and John Wesley follow the Syriac and Targum in reading it of holiness, that God is holy and just and true in all his works. On the wonders Adam Clarke distinguishes the observers: to the general observer God’s strength is most apparent, to the investigator of nature his wisdom, and to the genuine Christian his mercy and love. John Gill refers the redemption by the arm to Israel out of Egypt as a type of redemption by Christ, and Adam Clarke makes the argument explicit for the captives — as God delivered the fathers from Egypt, so we may expect deliverance from Chaldea, since the arm is not shortened that it cannot save.
16:
Adam Clarke thinks the sixteenth verse the most majestic thing he has found: God approaches the Red Sea, and the waters, seeing him, take fright and run off before him, dividing right and left to let him pass, while the deeps, uncovered and unable to fly, are filled with dismay — under such a poet, he says, inanimate nature springs into life and all is in motion. C.H. Spurgeon presses the contrast, that the water saw its God while man refuses to discern him, and that it was afraid while proud sinners fear not. Charles Ellicott renders the verb not were afraid but writhed, as in travail pains, and suggests the allusion is to the look that troubled the Egyptians. John Wesley has them stand still, as astonished men do. John Gill is careful that the waters are those of the Red Sea and not the Jordan.

The storm the psalm describes is not in the narrative of the Exodus, and the entry notices it. John Gill says plainly that these circumstances are not related by Moses in the history of the affair, but that, being recorded here by an inspired penman, there is no doubt of their truth; and he adds that Josephus relates the same things, that at the drowning of the Egyptians rains descended and there were terrible thunders, lightnings and thunderbolts. Adam Clarke counts four distinct things marked in these verses — the thunder in the sound sent out by the skies, the lightning in the arrows, the rain poured from the clouds, and an earthquake in the trembling of the earth — and infers a violent tempest at the passage. C.H. Spurgeon arms the elements, with the cloudy chariots hurrying to discharge their floods and the lightnings flying like bolts from the bow of God.

Charles Ellicott presses one word in the eighteenth verse: it means literally the vault, from a root meaning to roll, exactly as our own word derives, and he finds it strange that a rendering which so well suits the parallelism should have been set aside by modern scholars for whirlwind or rolling chariot wheels, the Greek and Latin having wheel, perhaps with the apparent revolution of the sky in mind. John Gill reaches the same picture by another route, taking the word for the orb, that is the air, so called because spherical. On the untraceable footsteps Adam Clarke says it was evident from the effects that God was there but his track could not be discovered, since he is without parts or limits and no object of sense, while John Wesley gives the plain reason that the water returned and covered them. Charles Ellicott quotes a modern historian at length to the same effect, that we do not know and need not know by what track the passage was effected, the obscuring being part of the lesson; and he defends the abrupt ending of the psalm, since no better close could be reached from the poet’s perplexity than the religious aids left by Moses and Aaron. Keil and Delitzsch call it the refrain-like close and note that the shepherd figure is as it were the monogram of these psalms, at which the poet stops and loses himself in the old history of redemption, which is to him a prophecy of the future.
